title: Unit of lighting and Convertion
abstract: A compact guide to lumen, candela, lux, luminance, and radiant power—with the geometry needed to convert between them correctly.
imageAlt: A relationship map connecting lumen, candela, lux, and candela per square metre
lede: Lighting units describe different parts of the same system: total visible output, directional strength, light arriving at a surface, and the brightness that a surface presents to an eye or camera. A valid conversion therefore needs the missing geometry—solid angle, distance, incidence angle, illuminated area, or projected emitter area.

sections.heading: The five quantities
paragraphs: Lumen, candela, lux, and candela per square metre are photometric units, so they describe light according to the sensitivity of human vision. Watt is radiometric: it measures physical optical power without applying that visual weighting.
These units are related, but they are not interchangeable labels for brightness. Each one answers a different question.

rows: Brightness of a surface seen by an eye or camera
Physical optical energy per unit time, not eye-weighted
technicalTables.caption: The quantity determines the unit; geometry determines whether a conversion is possible.

sections.heading: Lumen ↔ candela
paragraphs: Candela is luminous flux per solid angle. Converting a directional intensity into total lumens requires the angular distribution of the source.

For an isotropic point source, the emission fills 4π sr. This special case allows one candela value to determine the total luminous flux. Most real luminaires are not isotropic, so a single peak value from an IES profile cannot be treated as the total output.

callouts.title: Distribution is required
callouts.text: A directional IES value may reach 100,000 cd while the fixture’s total lumen output is much smaller than a 4π conversion would suggest. Integrate the full directional distribution instead of assuming isotropic emission.

sections.heading: Candela → lux
paragraphs: Illuminance from a point light follows the inverse-square law and the cosine of the incidence angle. Distance is measured from the light to the receiving point, and θ is the angle between the incoming light direction and the surface normal.
When the surface faces the light directly, θ is zero and the cosine term becomes one.

terms.text: Incidence angle from the surface normal.

technicalTables.caption: Values assume θ = 0. Doubling r reduces E to one quarter.

sections.heading: Lumen → lux
paragraphs: Lux is luminous flux per illuminated area. A direct conversion from lumens is valid only when the flux distribution and receiving area are known.
If 1000 lm is distributed uniformly over 10 m², the illuminance is 100 lx. A focused beam and a wide beam can have equal lumens but produce very different lux values on the same surface.

sections.heading: cd/m² and nit: visible surface brightness
paragraphs: Luminance describes how bright a surface appears in a direction. One nit is exactly one candela per square metre. It is different from illuminance: lux measures light arriving at a surface, while cd/m² measures the directional brightness leaving or emitted by that surface.

For a perfectly diffuse Lambertian surface, reflected luminance depends on illuminance and reflectance. A perfect white surface under 1000 lx reaches about 318 cd/m²; a darker surface produces proportionally less luminance.

callouts.title: Three viewpoints
callouts.text: cd describes source strength in a direction; lx describes light arriving at something; cd/m² describes how bright that thing appears.

sections.heading: Candela ↔ cd/m²
paragraphs: Directional intensity is luminance integrated over apparent emitting area. For a flat, uniform emitter viewed straight-on, luminance is intensity divided by physical area.

At an angle, use projected area. The cosine term reduces the apparent area as the emitter turns away from the viewing direction. This relationship is especially useful when an IES intensity must be connected to a finite emitter brightness.

equations.label: Projected emitter area
equations.expression: I = LAₚ    ·    Aₚ = A cosθ    ⇒    I = LA cosθ

sections.heading: A practical relationship map
paragraphs: The conversion path is a geometry problem. Solid angle links total flux to directional intensity; distance and incidence angle link intensity to illuminance; projected emitter area links intensity to luminance.
For UE and IES work, use the directional candela value I(θ, φ) from the IES table. Do not collapse total lumens into one candela value unless the angular distribution is explicitly defined.

technicalTables.caption: Every arrow names the geometric information required for the conversion.

equations.label: IES lighting chain
equations.expression: I(θ, φ)    →    E(r, θ)    →    L(ρ, Aₚ)
terms: IES cd → lx at a position → cd/m² of an illuminated or emissive surface

closing: Choose the quantity first, then supply the geometry. The symbols make the constraint visible: Φ needs Ω, I needs r and θ, and L needs ρ or Aₚ.
